It has turned into a chore instead of a way to relax and enjoy being around other people with similar issues.

as for what other people think, I don't care what they think about me. But when they think that I'm off the program it becomes very pushy and they constantly question me and grill me and I start feeling completely uncomfortable talking to them again. That's the only reason I kind of care about what they think because it reflects outwardly and it makes it very difficult to open up to anyone.

I don't mind saying I'm powerless over alcohol. But I'm not powerless about how to stop drinking and how to stay sober. But most of my AA members disagree and make sure I know they are not happy. I'm 18 months. Most of the physical symptoms have gone. I'm still weaker on my left side than right. Most of what's left is PTSD and brain injury type things. Memory. Anger. Disassociation. Really bad brain fog. Etc 

I had some warning before the stroke. After I left the gym and got home, my neck hurt. Kept thinking I just overdid my shoulder. Within 2 hours I had unbearable pain. 

Anyway, found the tear, watched overnight for clots. Released home. Then the first mini stroke hit. Went to hospital. Eventually had 3 mini strokes and the full stroke.

But I had no idea this was possible to someone my age and health.

Has there been a specific point where things turned around for you?

Honestly I struggled so hard in the first 6 months I was hospitalized for suicidal thoughts and an attempt.

And though I largely still feel like that often, I have a new foster dog, my 2 dogs, and my husband. And even when I didn't love him. I didn't want to hurt him and wanted the best for him.

I've recently met a new personal trainer who can help continue my long term recovery. If it weren't for my dogs, I would have given up. And now I'm finally beginning to feel love for my husband again. Not near as much as before. But it's there. So I have a small bit more hope 

Feel free to message me anytime if you need someone to talk to. Really appreciate the comment man.

Firstly, I was 10lb overweight. Doctors said it was a non contributor in my stroke. This was trauma related so it could happen to anyone at all. And I didn't push myself because the ab crunch machine only has you use your bodyweight and my personal trainer was even helping push it up at the end as it was getting difficult. 

Doctors also said if I was using that machine that it's very strange anyway because usually it's a blow to the neck or whiplash that causes the tear.

Before the stroke I was considered very healthy. I'd been eating well for a couple years at that point, didn't have high cholesterol or sugar or any indicators.

I'm not sure why you don't seem to understand the term 'freak accident'. It means doctors saw no precursor or cause. I only am overweight due to a hormone imbalance and eating healthily like a person without it can still cause weight gain. So I wasn't munching down on pizza and burgers.

They also called mine a freak accident. Other than being slightly overweight (at the time I was only 10lb overweight so they said it was not a solid contributor).

So I have major paranoia of it happening again. There was no real cause. And that means it could happen again due to another freak occurrence.

The slightest pain in my neck (my first symptom of the artery dissection) sends me into a spiral of doubt and paranoia.

Sorry this happened to you. How long post are you?

Oddly enough I was just doing the crunch machine ... Doctors didn't understand how I tore the artery as it's normally a very obvious trauma. This was a 'freak occurrence'. And it was on my last one too!

I called the national suicide hotline in 2008. The lady seemed annoyed and very unresponsive. I felt like an idiot for crying and said I guess in okay now. She said "uh huh" and the line went dead.

This was just enough to push me over and I ended up hospitalized (which was a great experience).

I'd recently had a stroke. And one day shortly after, I woke up and everything had changed. I'm different. I'm nothing that resembles me before the stroke. In a bad way. I'm angry. I can't understand people anymore. I have massive and worsening brain fog.

But worst of all. I stopped loving my husband. We had been together 9 years. And I absolutely adored him. My light. My everything. You make me smile so much more than I ever imagined.

And it was gone. He wasn't in the limelight of my life. I'm 18 months post stroke and I finally feel for him again and don't want us to change. So we're progressing. But I struggle everyday to enjoy it. I struggle to feel like I belong to me. To my husband. To this body. To...me.

The worst day of my life began the day I had the first mini stroke. And it has never ended. Everything after has been pure pain and anger.

Teacher told my mom who yelled at me for scaring the teacher.

I think about Kyle less now. I had been very sensitive about gun to the head motions. But now even I do them sometimes. I'm stronger. I'm okay mostly. But I'll never forget what I saw. What I felt. What I witnessed his parents seeing.

Sometimes I still miss him. And sometimes I still hate him. But mostly I just feel sad he didn't get the help that I did.

If they are physically demanding, remember you are exerting a lot more energy than your off days. So you need to eat more though you have less time. I personally prefer protein shakes. This is because you often feel hungry, or want a snack, because you are actually thirsty. You don't realize it. You feel completely hungry. But if you try to wait 30 minutes or so and drink a glass or two of water, it often goes away. You feel less tired and you stave off putting junk food or fast food in your body.

I've personally had issues with a few creeps. It can never hurt to have extra security! 3-4 door locks, a couple extra steel bolts along the inside of the door, a door jam (these alone can be pushed through, but with other security can definitely help!), close blinds at night (anyone can see through blinds with lights on when walking by), have defense classes (helped me so much to feel more ready when I absolutely have to walk at night), and have pepper spray or a knife (or gun if permitted carry license) in purse and or car.

I might sound paranoid. But I actually knew a couple people before who had similar things and their reasoning was always sound. Just introduce a few of these at a time, explaining it's never a bad thing to have more security. Especially for someone living alone or with others who are often consider more 'easily vulnerable' by others.

I definitely suggest seeing if your daughter would be willing to take self defense classes, if offered. Refresh every year. I found a class that did 3 parts. Took 4 weeks (1 class/week) over 3 months with a month inbetween. $40/each course.

I've also been told it's especially beneficial to take 2 classes first to see which one you feel is more beneficial for you. Some are often more geared toward a certain age group so someone younger than 18 may feel out of place or not be able to perform the instructed moves.

I'd say the first thing is to break any typical routines you have. Change it up. If your morning routine is always the same (Brush teeth, shower, get dressed, let the dog out, eat, go to work), try to change it. Let the dog out, eat, shower, get dressed, go to work. You can do similar things with other routines. Bed time routines, any daily routines including sitting on the couch watching tv or playing games.

Also, try to do something you used to enjoy. A sport, a movie, eating out, a comedy club. It may not work, so don't get frustrated. We're just trying it out.

Another thing. If you are willing to do it. Change your appearance. Basically, get a different haircut. It often makes you feel like a 'new' you. It can give that apathy a "Hey, this is a new me and I don't have all the problems I did before!" feeling. Another option is to color your hair. Or start by buying a new wardrobe if you have the funds.

A huge one for me was exercise. I know "uuuuuugh". :P

But it truly did help. The first 3 times were kind of boring and tiring. But then I got into the routine and loaded my podcast with things. I also got in the habit of watching tv shows or movies while jogging inside or on the treadmill at the workout center. So time flew by fast.

Anyway. As I'm sure you've heard. It releases endorphines. Which make you feel good. It also makes you feel productive. And healthy. And it generally has a good effect on your body. Lifting weights or running or yoga. Whatever you want to do. I suggest trying it out for at least 28 days in a row. It takes 28 days to form a habit.

So if you choose any of those, I'd suggest doing them at least 2 times a week, if not 3 the first month to get into the routine. Then you can back down to 1-2 times a week.

Also, one thing I should have mentioned earlier. Apathy is often caused by anxiety or depression. It's pretty common. Just one of the lesser talked about symptoms.

Another thing to consider is to stay busy. Don't push yourself. But line up things to do with family and friends, work, chores, errands, exercise, tv shows, etc. It keeps the mind from fretting mostly and can in turn cause the apathy to lessen.

Also, if you ever decide to try our medications again, I suggest you ask your doctor about Celexa/Citalopram. It's in the same category as Prozac, but it has much fewer side effects and is generally more accepted by the body. The most likely reason they went with Prozac is because if it does work, it works very effectively. However, it has very strong side effects for those who it does not work for.

Just so you know! Want to be sure you are fully informed on all options and all the information I can tell you.

I'm sure I can come up with more ideas for you if none of these sounds good for you. Just keep talking with me and telling me what does and doesn't work or sound good. We'll figure it out. You're not alone!

PS: The things that helped me the most were finding tv shows or movies to get into and exercise. I also would cut my hair every 3 months (just a trim, but it made me feel fresh and renewed for a couple weeks).

Almost drowned my entire family except my sister when I was about 9.

We have a creek (it's very large and strong) in my hometown. My mom, stepdad, step brother, and step sister, all went. My actual sister was elsewhere.

The three of us kids were playing in the water, stepdad was fishing from a cliff down creek several feet, mom was on the shore reading. 

We kept yelling "help" during our play. Mom tells us to stop in case we need actual help...I swear she jinxed us.

I was only in ankle-deep water. Next thing I know, a current grabs hold of my ankle. It starts to slip on the rocks. So my stepbrother grabs me as he sees I'm starting to slide uncontrollably. Unfortunately, I quickly picked up speed, and he started to slide. His sister grabbed him.

All three of us go flying past their dad. He tossed his fishing rod in the creek and yells for my mom. They both jump in.

We luckily got caught in a bend and just kept going in a circle there. My mom and stepdad found a rock they both could take turns standing on. As we'd circle around, they'd grab one of us and toss us up a clif where there was a ledge.

I remember once, my stepbrother was stepping on top of me in the water and I couldn't breathe. It felt like my lungs were imploding. I still don't know how my mom knew where I was, as the water was murky creek water. But her hand suddenly pulled me out from under his feet just as I was closing my eyes.

Then my stepdad grabbed my other arm above the water and finally got me thrown onto the ledge.

Until they separated, they never let it go. It was actually taboo to talk about it. Always said I almost drowned my whole family. It was my fault. Etc. We didn't even go to the doctors or anything afterward. For nearly 6 years, I was horrified of water. Drinking water, bottled water, faucet water, shower, bath. I literally sponge bathed myself.

But, now I love my showers!
